# Mahāmorajātaka (Ja 491)

**ID:** Ja 491  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Mahāmorajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul13.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul13.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

At the end of the narrative, following the revelation of the Four Noble Truths, the monk attains arahantship, and the Buddha identifies himself as the peacock king (*morarājā*) [Fausböll 1887].

Scholarly discussion also observes that the prose commentary mentions snakes among the perils from which the peacock remains free, comparing the figure of the peacock-king to related narratives such as the Suvarṇāvabhāsa account in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya [Schmithausen, Maitri magic].

**Sources**

- [Fausböll 1887] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 4 (1887) — Confirmed opening and concluding formulas, including the backsliding monk's realization of arahantship and the Bodhisatta identification.
- [Schmithausen, Maitri magic] Lambert Schmithausen, Maitrī and Magic: Aspects of the Buddhist Attitude Towards Dangerous Animals — Noted the commentary's mention of snake dangers and compared the text with peacock-king stories in Sanskrit Vinaya literature.
